According to Frank Holmes, Chairman of HIVE Digital Technologies, traditional Bitcoin mining is becoming far less profitable than AI computing. 🧐

This growing profitability gap is pushing some mining companies to diversify into AI infrastructure, renting GPU computing power instead of relying solely on Bitcoin mining.

📌 Hidden Fees: Why “Zero Fee” Doesn’t Mean Free

Main Points
⏺ Crypto trade costs can hide in spreads, slippage, and execution routes
⏺ “No fee” often means the cost moves somewhere else
⏺ This post explains how to see the real price of an action

1️⃣ Spread — the gap between buy and sell price can already be your first hidden cost.
2️⃣ Slippage — weaker liquidity pushes your final price away from the quote.
3️⃣ Routing — an app or aggregator may choose a route that benefits it more than you.
4️⃣ Network Costs — even if the platform charges no fee, gas is still a real expense.
5️⃣ Practical Rule — compare final received amounts, check multiple routes, and don’t trust “0% fee” alone.

Final Thoughts

Trades are rarely free. If the fee isn’t visible in one line, it may live inside price, routing, or liquidity.

Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, issued the warning. Continued US naval pressure "will both tighten the lock on the Strait of Hormuz and close other straits and bottlenecks," he said. 

"The global economy, the energy market, and American voters will pay the price," according to Iran's Fars News Agency. Note who's footing the bill in that sentence. Not Washington's decision-makers. Whoever's stuck paying at the pump in November.

A senior security official went further with Tasnim. He called US media reports of imminent strikes "a kind of madness." Then he immediately described, in detail, the madness Iran has planned in response. 

"We have prepared a comprehensive plan to respond that includes targeting the vital infrastructure of Israel and the US energy infrastructure in the region and we are ready for it," he said. 

He cited Iran's performance in "the 40-day war" as proof of both "ability and will," APA reports. 

Denouncing the premise while confirming the plan is a neat trick. It works exactly once before everyone just calls it a threat.

Then IRGC-linked Fars News did something new. It published an actual target list. 

The list named Saudi Arabia's Ghawar field, the UAE's Ruwais refinery and Zakum field, Qatar's Ras Laffan LNG terminal, Kuwait's Burgan field, and Bahrain's Sitra refinery, Iran International reports. It also named Israel's Tamar and Leviathan gas fields. That's a first. 

Israel hadn't appeared on Iran's target lists since the American strikes began five months ago. Every Gulf monarchy that has spent years hedging between Washington and Tehran just got told, in print, exactly what a miscalculation costs them. Israel just got added to a list it had managed to stay off of.

So the message lands everywhere at once. To Riyadh and Abu Dhabi: don't assume neutrality buys immunity. To Washington: don't assume this stays contained to Iranian soil. 

To Israel: welcome to the list. Iran didn't have to fire a shot to make half the region recalculate its risk exposure this weekend. Who exactly gets to sit this one out?
